verdict: Caution on Angul coal mining and washeries: lend only to contracted, cash-backed operators; the data pack gives no score, so treat this as a hold-and-select call, not a green light.
title: Angul coal mining & washeries: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Coal mining and washing is a tonnage business: you dig, you crush and wash, you move tonnes by road and rail, and you get paid per tonne by a buyer who is usually a power plant or a sponge-iron unit.** Cash is made on the spread between extraction or purchase cost and the washed-coal sale price, minus the freight to the railway siding. In Angul the physical bottleneck is the road-to-rail link: SCCL has deposited Rs. 350 mn for the Chandipara-Jarapada bypass road meant to connect Naini block coal to the Jarapada railway junction [2]. **So when a proposal lands, check which siding the borrower actually evacuates through; if the answer is a road still under construction, ask for the completion date and the fallback route.**

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in washed, higher-grade coal, not raw pithead output.** BCCL's own plan is to raise sale of beneficiated coal by renovating ageing washeries and commissioning new ones with a combined capacity of 7.00 million tonnes per year [10]. The working-capital cycle is the killer: one rated coal trader pays suppliers in advance and recovers from customers in around 45-60 days, funding the gap with working-capital bank borrowings [8]. **So on every proposal, map the advance-to-collection gap; if the borrower is paying advance to a linked supplier, ask for the supplier's name and the last six months of payments.**

## What has changed now
**The local news is about a new pithead power plant and land, not about coal demand.** SCCL has asked the Angul district administration for land near the Naini mine for a pithead thermal plant, plus land for a resettlement colony for 40 displaced families [2]. Peer results are better: Coal India's Q2FY27 production was 151 MT, up 4% YoY, and October 2026 output recovered [6][7]. BCCL's October update shows production up 7% and offtake up 11%, but cumulative fiscal-year production is still negative [4]. **So treat the peer numbers as a sign that volumes are returning, not as proof that Angul washeries are full; ask each borrower for their own monthly washed-tonne dispatch.**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue washery operators with a written offtake contract to a named power or steel buyer, and transporters with a railway-siding linkage.** Avoid pure traders with no washing asset and no contract, and avoid anyone whose evacuation depends on the two bypass roads still being built [2]. Structure against receivables: **take monthly washed-tonne dispatch, railway rakes loaded, and the receivables-ageing every month; if receivables past 60 days cross a fifth of sales, stop fresh limits.** The data pack gives no score for this city or state [D], so the call rests on first principles and peers. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch the road, the rake and the buyer.** If the Jarapada link slips, stock piles up and cash stops. If the buyer is a single state power plant, payment delays hit fast. If the borrower's own fiscal-year output is negative like BCCL's cumulative figure [4], the monthly growth is noise.

## What I want in the file
**A one-page cash map per borrower: advance paid, days to collect, tonnes washed, rakes loaded, and the buyer's name.** No file leaves your desk without it. The Angul-specific public record is thin, so lean on the borrower's own numbers and the peer benchmarks above.

## The call
**Caution, not avoid.** The sector's volumes are improving [4][6][7] and a new pithead plant is being discussed [2], but the data pack has no score [D] and the local news is about land, not cash. Lend to contracted washers and siding-linked transporters; decline unhedged traders.
